pos.personaBrief: Cullis wanted territory, not possession: 'every pass decisive and long rather than pretty and short', ball into the opponent's third, with fast counter-style breaks (Flowers 1962, Honved counter-attacks). Wolves did not hand the ball over on purpose, they won it fast and went forward.

pro.personaBrief: Cullis's plan: ball into the penalty area in a maximum of three passes, full-backs find a forward, short cross-field passes disapproved, Reep's ban on square passes. Wolves played the long ball to fast wingers and ignored risky short build-up.

est.personaBrief: Wolves played a WM-based 2-3-5 with defined roles, wingers on the touchline and a centre-forward upfield; attacks were direct long passes, not tight combinations. Broadbent as an advanced winger was a stratagem, but the base shape was fixed.

lar.personaBrief: Wingers were central to the style: long balls into space for Hancocks and Mullen, Hooper the 'ideal winger', Broadbent used as an advanced winger to isolate full-backs (Cullis 1960, TFT, Game of the People).

blo.personaBrief: Rapid tackling by every player, forwards included, to win the ball before the opponent controls it; Honved 'swarm everywhere', 'tighten the screws'. High, aggressive ball-winning, not a low block.

mar.personaBrief: No source states the marking scheme; from the WM-era norm (centre-half on centre-forward, full-backs on wingers) and aggressive tackling, Wolves is judged mostly man-oriented, with this being memory-based.

pla.personaBrief: Wolves had one imposed identity: tempo beyond the opposition, kick-and-rush accepted as a label, a same plan at half-time (Honved: more of the same long passes). Cullis briefed on opponents, but only as detail on top of his own plan.

res.personaBrief: Puritan winner who built a results-driven, utilitarian style, relying on fitness and aggression, unbothered by being called unpopular or dirty; yet attacking, not defensive, with 100 goals a season and no settling for draws.

sis.personaBrief: A drilled collective plan with every player having a function, fitness targets and tackling duties even for forwards; wingers were pace specialists inside the system, with no freedom for stars.

jog.personaBrief: Cullis 'placed huge emphasis on fitness and power', trained until it hurts, wanted fast, direct wingers and tacklers; Wolves lacked superior technique and valued duels and pace.

bas.personaBrief: Mixed: the Wath Wanderers nursery club, FA Youth Cup finals and 17-year-old Broadbent, but also record fees (Hooper) and veterans like Wright and Slater in title teams. Winning, not development, was the goal.

lid.personaBrief: Cullis was a strict disciplinarian ('we all hated his guts', 'tough disciplinarian'), knew what he wanted, no large-scale inquests, with authority over everyone including Billy Wright.
